issues.line_text: My grandmother's trust fund covered the basics, stretched carefully across rent, travel, equipment.
issues.description: Story Bible states Josh's adoptive parents are 'the Caines' - this should reference them, not a grandmother. If the trust is from his birth family, it needs clarification. If from adoptive grandmother, should say 'my grandmother Caine' or similar.
issues.fix: The trust fund my adoptive parents set up covered the basics, stretched carefully across rent, travel, equipment.
issues.rationale: Clarifies the source of the trust fund without introducing new family members not established in Story Bible. Maintains financial independence backstory while staying consistent with known family structure.

issues.line_text: My agent thinks I'm having a midlife crisis at thirty.
issues.description: Josh is 29 in October 2024 (born 1995, was 3 in 1998). This was previously fixed in Chapter 1 from 'midlife crisis at thirty' to 'quarter-life crisis at twenty-nine.' Same error appears here.
issues.fix: My agent thinks I'm having a quarter-life crisis at twenty-nine.
issues.rationale: Maintains consistency with Josh's established age (29) and mirrors the fix already applied in Chapter 1. 'Quarter-life crisis' is age-appropriate for late twenties.

issues.line_text: Just tired. Just a heavy meal on top of too much wine. That's all.
issues.description: This is Josh's internal rationalization for drowsiness after dinner. While he SHOULD dismiss the drugging possibility (since Eleanor isn't actually drugging him), the phrasing 'Just tired. Just... That's all.' creates a repetitive defensive pattern that might draw too much reader attention to the possibility. More natural to dismiss it once.
issues.fix: Just tired. Heavy meal, too much wine.
issues.rationale: More casual dismissal that doesn't overemphasize the drugging possibility. Josh genuinely IS just tired/tipsy here, so his internal voice should be more matter-of-fact, not defensively reassuring himself.

issues.line_text: I'd known Eleanor for what, five days? Six?
issues.description: Chapter is dated October 28. Eleanor's Chapter 2 and Josh's Chapter 1 are both October 22 (arrival day). October 22 to October 28 is 6 days. Josh should be more certain about this count since he's an investigative journalist who tracks details.
issues.fix: I'd known Eleanor for what, six days?
issues.rationale: Math correction (Oct 22-28 = 6 days). Removes uncertainty that doesn't fit Josh's character as someone who meticulously tracks timelines and dates in his investigation.

issues.line_text: When I reached my bedroom, I checked my watch: 11:34 PM. Wait. We'd finished dinner at... eight? Eight-thirty?
issues.description: The phrasing suggests Josh is trying to account for missing time (implying drugging/fugue state). However, per Story Bible, Josh's first blackout shouldn't occur until 'Early Dec' (Act 2). In late October, he should just be tired from wine, not experiencing time gaps that make him suspicious.
issues.fix: When I reached my bedroom, I checked my watch: 11:34 PM. Later than I'd planned, but the conversation had flowed so easily I'd lost track of time.
issues.rationale: Removes the implication of suspicious missing time. Josh can lose track of time due to engaging conversation and wine without it reading as a blackout. Maintains the intimacy of the evening without introducing fugue-state symptoms too early.

notes: Chapter is generally clean. The dinner scene appropriately shows Josh falling for Eleanor while maintaining his investigative suspicions. The abandoned campsite discovery is a good plant. Eleanor's loft explanation (grief storage from Seattle teaching job) is an effective misdirection that will recontextualize later. The age error ('thirty' vs 'twenty-nine') is the same issue previously fixed in Ch1, suggesting a need to verify this across all chapters. The 'grandmother's trust fund' is a new detail not in Story Bible and needs author confirmation or revision.
